statement: Built with MSBuild from the Visual Studio project, in Debug and Release configurations. A batch script stamps the Git description as the version first. A GitHub Actions workflow named Build Latest builds the Release executable automatically; its release target is not readable here. There is no test project.

assumed.why: The build badge names the workflow, but its steps and where it publishes are in a file this answer does not cite.
assumed.ifWrong: The automated build may run different steps or publish elsewhere, so how releases reach users would differ.

evidence.shows: Build badge links to the Build Latest GitHub Actions workflow.
Debug and Release build configurations.
Writes the Git description into the version file before building.
Manual build steps in Visual Studio.

statement: Nothing runs around every action: no sign-in, request pipeline or interceptor. At launch the operating system applies the manifest's elevation request. When policy sources open and when saving, the program reports whether each source is writable.

evidence.shows: Manifest requests highest available privilege at launch.
Reports each source's writability after opening.
Save checks writability of each source.

statement: One edit: the person opens a policy, the dialog changes an in-memory copy, then File | Save writes it. Only writable sources are saved. Local policy writes the file, then refreshes Windows policy or copies the difference into the registry. Per-user policy refreshes. A policy file is only written to disk; live registry is already applied; an offline user hive applies on close.

evidence.shows: Save writes comments and writable sources, stores choices, shows a message.
Local policy save writes file, refreshes or applies difference.
Registry, offline hive, null and policy-file sources do different things.
Per-user policy save writes file and refreshes policy.

statement: It runs on the user's own Windows machine, as a 32- or 64-bit process on a .NET Framework 4.x runtime built for 4.5.2, editing that machine's registry and policy files. It hosts no service; its only outside call is the optional definitions download from Microsoft.

evidence.shows: Windows executable targeting .NET Framework 4.5.2.
Accepts any 4.x runtime, built for 4.5.2.
Requires .NET Framework 4.5.2 or newer on Windows.
Fixed download address at download.microsoft.com and a fixed path inside the package for one Windows 11 release.

statement: The program is built against .NET Framework 4.5.2, a version Microsoft no longer supports. It still runs on newer 4.x runtimes, but its build target receives no fixes.

evidence.shows: Targets .NET Framework 4.5.2.
Accepts any 4.x runtime.

externalSource.source: Microsoft support lifecycle for .NET Framework 4.5.2, which ended support in April 2022

statement: The definitions download fetches a Microsoft installer over HTTPS from one fixed address and runs it with no checksum or signature check, trusting that host alone. Into the chosen destination (default the Windows policy folder) it moves files; for an administrator it replaces owner and permissions on that folder and the files.

evidence.shows: Downloads the installer and runs msiexec on it without verification.
If the destination exists and user is administrator, takes ownership; moves files in.
Replaces permissions on moved files and new folders.
Destination defaults to the Windows policy definitions folder and is editable.

statement: Saving can report success when nothing was saved: a source that is not writable is skipped, yet the message still says Success and names it not writable. A failed comment save is ignored. A person can believe an edit to such a source was kept.

evidence.shows: Skips non-writable sources, then always shows Success with status.
Comment save errors are ignored.
Writability is tested by trial write to the policy key.
